utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, ladies and gentlemen; good morning to our technicians, interpreters; good morning to our legal assistants, court reporters, representatives of the Registry; good morning to the representatives of the Prosecution: Mr. Harmon, Mr. Cayley, Mr. McCloskey; good morning to the Defence counsel: Mr. Petrusic, Mr. Visnjic; good morning, General Krstic. Good morning, General Dannatt. We have come back to continue with your testimony. I hope that you have had a good rest and that you are ready to continue. However, before we continue with the witness, I should like to hear from the Prosecutor, perhaps Mr. Harmon, and to ask him to review his position regarding the documents. We would like to know what are the documents that you really wish to tender under seal and what are the remaining documents. So perhaps with the assistance of Madam Registrar it would be convenient to rethink the issue and then we will make the ruling later on. Now, without much further ado, we will continue with the testimony of General Dannatt. Mr. Cayley, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, Mr. Petrusic, Mr. Visnjic. A small point arises, Your Honour. The witness would very much like to finish with his evidence today. Certain urgent matters have arisen for him in the UK requiring his attention. Whilst he has emphasised to me that he is entirely at the disposal of the Court and also bearing in mind that the cross-examination of the Defence cannot be limited in any way, would it be possible for us to continue until 3.00 today to finish the General's evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Would 3.00 be enough, Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I will do my best to finish my examination-in-chief in the first session, and Mr. Visnjic has indicated to me that the Defence possibly have two hours of cross-examination. The witness is prepared to stay until tomorrow, Your Honour, but if we could finish today, that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to ask the registrar if it is possible to work until 3.30 if it is necessary. In principle, we will go until 3.00; however, if it is necessary, I should like to continue until half past three. I think that we always have a representative of the interpreters here. I don't know if there's going to be a problem with that. We will have a break for lunch. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I will talk to the necessary persons dealing with the transcripts and security and see if it's a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then after the break -- yes, okay. Mr. Cayley, we will then work until 3.00. If it is necessary to prolong the day, we will work until 3.30 so as not to have the witness come back tomorrow. I hope you will not waste your time. Please proceed with the examination, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I realise much of this is dependent on my speed so I will go as efficiently as I can, and I thank the Court for allowing us to continue beyond our normal time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, I wish to briefly return to Prosecutor's Exhibit 459, which is a report from Colonel Jankovic of the Main Staff to the Intelligence Department of the Drina Corps, so an officer from a superior headquarters reporting to a subordinate headquarters. Can you explain to the Judges what, if anything, this document demonstrates to you? I've placed Exhibit 398 next to you so that that can assist you.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, good morning. Just in answer to that question, I would like to refer back, if I may, to an answer I gave yesterday when I introduced this particular diagram which showed the relationship between a subordinate command's intelligence and security functional area and the Higher Command's intelligence and security functional area, and indicated that orders were followed up the solid line, as it were, from the division to the corps and the corps to the division. That was the way that orders were passed. But it was perfectly legitimate in armies generally for there to be an informal functional chain, not of command but of exchange of information and advice from the subordinate to the superior and vice versa. Therefore, this particular exhibit, which is the one that Mr. Cayley has just referred to, from Colonel Jankovic of the Main Staff, the Security Branch, to the Drina Corps Intelligence Department is an illustration of that process actually taking place between the security or intelligence function at the division level having an exchange of information with the Intelligence and Security Branch, functional branch, at the corps level. This is an illustration of what I was talking about yesterday. I also notice and just draw your attention to the last part here. There's a postscript that says: "I think that if we want to take over the enclaves of Zepa and Gorazde ..." and it goes on. I would just draw attention to the words "I think that if ..." Well, if Colonel Jankovic, a Colonel on the Corps Staff, was actually giving orders to someone in the subordinate formation's Intelligence Department, I wouldn't have expected to see words like, "I think that if we want to ..." He would say something much more direct like, "You are to ..." I think this illustrates the linkage between the divisional Intelligence and Security Staff and the Corps Intelligence and Security Staff was one of advice and information as opposed to one of ordering. I believe that is the import behind this, and of course the substance of the message here is informing that the operation to take over the former enclave of Srebrenica had been completed, as I mentioned yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, in explaining this document you were using the nomenclature of NATO; you were referring to "corps" and "division." Just to clarify, Colonel Jankovic was on the Main Staff, which you equate with the corps, and he was actually sending information to the Drina Corps, which you've equated, with your language, to a division; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's exactly so. I was using this diagram here, and in this situation, we have the Drina Corps in this box effectively and the Main Staff in this box, but the principle that I was describing is exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness can be provided with Prosecutor's Exhibit 483.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, this is a document that's been provided to you by the Prosecutor. It's the combat order for operations in Zepa. You've read this document. What comments do you have for the Judges on this particular document? The document is dated the 13th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document is quite clearly the operation order produced by the Drina Corps Command for the operation to attack and capture the enclave of Zepa. Having reviewed it, it's a very good piece of Operational Staff work. It sets out very clearly the situation pertaining at the time; it sets out the mission, the intention to move towards and to attack Zepa; it details the subordinate units, brigades principally, of the Drina Corps that are to take part in this operation; and it gives a certain amount of coordinating instruction to make that attack happen. As I say, it is a very clear and well-organised and produced piece of Operational Staff work, which, frankly, is the sort of thing I would expect from competent and well-trained staff officers. And I notice that it's signed by General Krstic on the 13th of July, and he signed it as Chief of Staff. And having reviewed his military education and background, I'm not at all surprised that I see a piece of quality staff work of this nature. However, of particular interest to me is that while this particular operation was directed towards Zepa, and I'm also aware and we discussed yesterday that not only was there follow-up action going on around Srebrenica but that there was the business of moving the large number of civilians from Potocari back to behind Muslim lines, and there was also the issue of the Muslim military column of 28th Division, so there was a lot going in the Drina Corps area. But I notice in this document, at the end, that the Drina Corps forward command post mentioned here was to move to Krivace, which was in the section of Zepa, and it should start work at 1800 hours on the 13th of July, and that communications should be ready for the attack at 0600 hours on the 14th of July. So what that says to me is that the planning for this operation on Zepa would probably have gone on in the main Drina Corps command post. It would have been activity coordinated by the Chief of Staff. The Intelligence Staff, the Operation Staff, the Logistics Staff, would all have had a hand in putting together this operation. The order would have been drawn together by the Chief of Staff who then signed it, and the Commander who was going to command the operation would have moved or intended to move to the forward command post, as I said, at Krivace, but that communications would be in place by 0600 on the 14th of July. What that says to me is that although the commander is going to command this operation from the forward command post at Krivace, a communications back to the main command post would have been established, and, therefore, that commander would have been in touch and aware of all the other activities going on within his corps area of responsibility, and I just mentioned a number those major activities which I'm aware were also going on at the same time, as well as the developing plans for the attack on Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, one point from paragraph 10. It states that: "The Drina Corps forward command post will be in Krivace and shall start work at 1800 hours on the 13th of July, 1995." Would it be right to assume that it would be the Corps Commander, the Corps Commander of the Drina Corps, who would have been at that command post after its establishment on the 13th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would expect that to be the case. I think yesterday, in my earlier evidence, I talked about in a division such as mine or a corps such as the Drina Corps, that there are a number of headquarters. There is the main headquarters where the majority of the staff are and where the Chief of Staff usually is, where planning is conducted, and where operations, in the main, are controlled from. But that at certain times a forward command post or a tactical command post can be established, usually to which the commander, the overall commander, deploys in order to command the immediate operation. So what I see here is, from the Main Headquarters at another location, this forward command post, I would call it a tactical command post, is established close to the new operation for the Corps Commander to coordinate the attack from there. Another point which has just caught my eye on the screen is, again, as I referred yesterday, daily records describing the situation at 1700 hours to be submitted at 1800 hours were required. So, again, we've got this business that I would expect in a properly organised military formation, of reminding everyone that daily combat records from the brigades were required in order to keep the headquarters fully informed of all the situations throughout the corps area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could now be provided with Exhibit 463.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I want to move on, General, with the interception and the mopping up of the mixed the military-civilian column that left Srebrenica. You're aware of this event. First of all, Exhibit 463, which is an order signed by General Krstic, what type of order is this? This document is dated the 13th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is an order, and it's an order instituting another operation, effectively a security operation, a search operation, in what I would describe as the rear area, away from the main combat zone perhaps, of the corps. In this order, General Krstic, now signing a notice as Commander of the corps, I'm reminded of the previous operation, of the previous order we were looking at a moment ago, signed on the same date by General Krstic as Chief of Staff. So that tells me that something has changed on that day, but, nevertheless, this operation is a separate operation ordered by General Krstic to identify, capture, and round up a number of people who have escaped from the former Srebrenica enclave. And the way, I think in general terms, I would characterise this operation is as a rear operation. If I could just generalise, in principle, for a moment. Military operations, on the whole, are categorised either formally or informally as deep, close, or rear operations. Deep operations are those things which are done to prepare the ground, to change the circumstances ahead of time to give a better prospect of your close operation, when you're actually applying your combat power, for that to happen successfully. For example, going back to issues we were discussing yesterday, the preliminary bombardment of Srebrenica and the fear that that engendered amongst the people. I would see that as a deep operation activity, trying to change the terms for future combat. Then when the Drina Corps units attacked Srebrenica, that was the close operation. What we see here is a rear operation, essentially a security operation being conducted to ensure the security and protection of the remaining Drina Corps troops, to make sure that civilians in the area were protected from military people still roaming in that rear area. So I see this as a rear operation. And deep, close, and rear operations are sometimes conducted in sequence. Sometimes they are conducted at the same time. What these two documents, this one and the previous one we looked at, indicate to me, that at this time, the Drina Corps was concerned with a deep and close operation focus towards accident, and we have this rear operation focused to the area generally around part of Srebrenica towards Zvornik and the other places are mentioned here in this order. So a lot, as I've said before, was going on in the Drina Corps area, but for a properly organised corps and headquarters such as I believe the Drina Corps to have been, under good command, a number things going on does not present a problem. They're capable of looking in several directions, doing several things at the same time, all coordinated by the main headquarters, as I said, where the Chief of Staff would be presiding and keeping the commander, now probably at the forward command post, in the picture about everything that was going on in his corps area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Can I just ask one question?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Does the terrain that's referred to in paragraphs 1 and 2 of this order, that's going to be the object of the mop-up or the search, does that roughly encompass the area or any of the area that the column was going to be marching down or is that more the kind of normal mop-up you would have expected after the fall of Srebrenica when they thought ---or at least there's some evidence that they thought that the 28th Brigade was still down by the Bandera Triangle, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, in general terms, the bits of geography referred to here are a little south of where the 28th Division column, we now know, was going north, although, they may not have known that or realised that at the time. Hence, I've made several references to there was a lot going on in the Drina Corps area at the time. It was actually quite a challenging moment for a commander and his staff, I would judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: But this particular -- if you read this, you read it with reference to what you would have thought was a normal mop-up operation after Srebrenica, extrinsic of the fact that you had a whole new conceivable breakthrough. The last question is: Would it have been normal procedure for these people to wear special identifying material? Paragraph 5: "Shall wear a white band on their right shoulder."

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite an intriguing point. I think it's quite a sensible and clever point. I think by this stage of the war, not everyone had a regular uniform. I think there was probably a genuine possibility of mistake and muddle because, after all, in search-type operation, you've got people over a large area, some of whom are on your side, some are on the other side, and I think to have ordered some particular distinctive identification mark was a sensible precaution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, now I'd like you to address from universal principles the operation to search the area and to intercept this column and to indicate on the chart in front of you the Staff Branches that you believe would have been involved in controlling this kind of operation.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you'd allow me to move to the ... Your Honours, rather as I indicated yesterday, an operation such as we're talking about now, which is the operation to identify, to find, the 28th Division column and then to reduce it, would require a coordination from a number of parts of the Corps. Not shown on here necessarily are the units. What we have here is the Staff and here we have subordinate units. In fact, they are shown here on the bottom, subordinate units. A number of brigades would have been told that they had some responsibility to take part in this action. So we've got a number of brigades being told that it is likely that in their area, particularly the Zvornik Brigade, it is likely that in their area this column will be passing. But because no one at that stage knows exactly where it is, I would see the Intelligence Section having a major role to play in this operation to try and find the enemy. I would see the Operations Section here having a major role to play to coordinate the activities of the various brigades and make sure that there was sufficient men available. I referred yesterday to the importance of the use of reserves, and I think in a situation like this where you don't know where the enemy is, the first corps function in any operation is to find the enemy. Once you've found him, then the next corps function is to fix him, in other words, to remove the enemy's freedom to manoeuvre, and then you've got to put together another force whereby you can strike him. So in general principles, operations are conducted to find, to fix, and to strike an enemy, and that requires a force to do each of those three key functions. Hence, the Intelligence part would have a large part of the coordination as, indeed, the Operations Section would as well in coordinating the activity of these various subordinates. Of course, if this operation goes on for any length of time, we're then looking support from the Rear Services area. The Transportation Service would have been required to move prisoners that were rounded up and captured. There is a responsibility on the Quartermaster Service to make sure that food was available for the potentially large numbers of prisoners. Indeed, Medical Services here would have been required to ensure that at least basic first-aid was provided under the terms of the Geneva Convention to prisoners that had been captured. Of course, I've talked about just now this operation being a rear operation, a security operation, a force protection operation, and therefore the Department for Security, Colonel Popovic, I think, would have had a fairly key interest in this to make sure that the security of the Drina Corps was maintained. So the deduction that I would make, within the general principle of an operation to find the enemy, then to fix him, to remove his ability to manoeuvre against you, and then to produce a force to strike would have required a coordination from a large number of the elements of the Drina Corps Staff and subordinate units. Not surprisingly, I can't conceive that being done other than with considerable coordination from the Corps Headquarters, the Chief of Staff, and of course incumbent on that is that the Commander, whoever he was and wherever he was, would be kept very firmly in command. Also, I've seen a particular series of situation reports, particularly from the Zvornik Brigade who became very concerned about this operation when it looked as if the column might actually be going to make an attack on Zvornik, when the Commander of the Zvornik Brigade particularly appealed to the Corps Commander and said, "You must take me away and some of my men from the attack on Zepa. We need to get back to the Zvornik area because we've got a serious problem going on." So that shows to me that coordination within the Corps was absolutely vital and that the Commander and the Chief of Staff were absolutely essential to the decision-making process of how to deal with that 28th Division column, which, as I've said several times, I think would have presented a major headache in the Drina Corps area at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be provided with Exhibit 464.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General, this is an order from the Bratunac Brigade of the 14th of July, 1995. Rather than having you do it because the document speaks for itself, this is an order, Your Honours, that directly references Exhibit 463, the order from General Krstic. It, indeed, refers to the order of General Krstic of the 13th of July, 1995. General, what conclusion - perhaps it speaks for itself - can you draw from the fact that Colonel Blagojevic is essentially issuing an order directly in response to General Krstic's order to his own subordinate battalions to conduct this search of the terrain?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's exactly the deduction I draw from this document. In the opening three lines here, the Brigade Commander of the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade makes reference to the fact that he has received an order from the Drina Corps, dated the 13th of July, and he is now issuing his own orders to his own battalions. "The 1st Infantry Battalion will search ..." and he's giving them all various details. "The 2nd Infantry Battalion will search ..." and so it goes on. "The 3rd Infantry Battalion will search ..." What this simply shows to me is a properly functioning chain of operational command. The Drina Corps issued an operation; it was received by one of the brigades, in this case, the Bratunac Brigade. The Commander has analysed that order; he's thought about it, he's made his own plan, and he's now issuing orders to his own battalions in order to comply with that order originally issued by the Drina Corps. This is showing to me a joined up and properly functioning command and control and operational planning process.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 488.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General, the previous document was an order from Colonel Blagojevic, and here is a daily combat report actually issued on the 13th of July of 1995 to the Drina Corps Command. This document discusses a search that is taking place. What can you say about this particular document?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, there are a number of comments that I would make about this. First of all, it's issued by the Command of the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade; it's being sent to the Command of the Drina Corps. It calls itself, interestingly, a daily combat report and the content of it gives an update of operational activity going on in the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade area. And it's following the format that I've seen in several of these orders. Interestingly, although the first three paragraphs give detail of what is going on, and that detail, I think, is not necessarily relevant, we then go on to paragraphs 4, 5, 6, and 7 and they're in very standard format. Paragraph 4: "There were no unexpected events." Paragraph 5 always seems to be a statement on morale within his unit, where all is good. Then paragraph 6 says that the logistics support is functioning well, and paragraph 7 reports casualties: "We've had no losses or wounded." We see that format in many of these daily combat reports, and it's a very efficient way of doing business. What catches my eye slightly is that -- yes, it's signed by the -- issued by the Brigade Commander, or in his name, signed by one of his staff officers and that's perfectly normal. But it's not at 1700 to be there at 1800, it's issued at 1545; it's probably by way of an interim combat report. But it's following the standard format of all the reports. Again, that indicates to me that the reporting system was functioning well within the Drina Corps, and there was a good flow of useful information finding its way from the lower levels, from the brigades, up to the Drina Corps Headquarters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Excuse me. Doesn't paragraph 1 up there: "The last large enemy group has been successfully encircled in the area of Konjevic Polje/Kasaba ..." doesn't that indicate to us that that was sort of the beginning of -- that was certainly one of the first incidents, massive incidents, that we're engaged with here?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: There's a little bit of tension in the thing between "no unexpected events" and "a large group." And then the second line in the second one: "The Brigade Command is working on a company to be sent to the area of the school to carry out the assignment ..." Anyway ...

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're absolutely right. It's often a feature of military situation reports that people tend to say things are going perhaps a little bit better than they really are. So when in paragraph 4 he said, "There are no unexpected events," most commanders want to show that they have got the whole thing thoroughly under control and that they're not being surprised by anything. So that doesn't, in itself, surprise me, although your point is right that the large enemy group around the Konjevic Polje/Kasaba area, we now know was one of the first of the groups from the 28th Division. But I would suspect that at this stage they were still trying to piece the jigsaw together and their picture was not that clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be provided with two exhibits together, 540 and 597.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General, we're moving to the Zvornik Infantry Brigade. 540 is a daily combat report of the 13th of July and 597 is a daily combat report of the 15th of July. Do these documents also show that the brigades were reporting to the Corps that they were engaged in combat with the Muslim column that was moving up towards and out of their area?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This report from the Zvornik Brigade is more complex. It's got more detail in it. I've already alluded to the fact that the Zvornik Brigade was pretty much in the eye of the storm as far as all this is concerned, and it's giving fairly detailed reporting here of various engagements that elements of the brigade had had with, quite clearly, the column of the 28th Division. But I think the general point, I don't think the detail of what is going on here is that relevant, but the general point is that I see a clear combat report from one of the subordinate brigades to the Drina Corps Headquarters drawing attention to what was going on in the area and making a fairly accurate and full report about it, again showing that the command and control process within the Corps was very much functioning in an effective and efficient way.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Indeed, there's no necessity to put 597 onto the ELMO, I will simply summarise what it says. Essentially it records the fact that Bosnian army forces were launching a heavy artillery attack into the area, and then it goes on to say that the Zvornik Brigade units were involved in cutting off and destroying Muslim forces retreating from Srebrenica in the direction of Tuzla. Again, does this demonstrate that the Corps was receiving regular information about what was happening within its subordinate brigades?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very much so. All these reports of a similar type make exactly that point, that good information, useful information, as far as the Corps Headquarters was concerned, was being passed to them by their subordinate brigades and would have given the Corps Headquarters a very clear picture of what was going on. I've made reference a couple of times to the fact that the Zvornik Brigade was very much in the thick of all this, and it doesn't surprise me at all that subsequently the Commander of the Zvornik Brigade asks for reinforcements because he was clearly under, really, quite a lot of pressure in his area at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 609, please. And if you could have ready 404/7, tab 430.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, the one particular paragraph that I'm interested in on this combat report, and it's dated the 15th of July from the Zvornik Brigade to the Command of the Drina Corps, is, and I'll read it: "An additional burden for us is the large number of prisoners distributed throughout schools in the brigade area as well as obligations of security and restoration of the terrain." Now, purely from general principles, and I don't want you to interpret what this means, but if you were a commander of a corps, would this not indicate to you, if you were receiving this report, that there were large numbers of prisoners in your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's exactly the meaning from the words that I see here, "An additional burden for us is the large number of prisoners distributed throughout schools in the brigade area ..." This doesn't tell me where those prisoners have come from, but noting again it's the Zvornik Brigade, I can fully understand why the Commander later on in this situation report, this combat report, asks for reserves. He's actually fighting the 28th Division column himself and taking prisoners, and it seems to be slightly to his surprise that a large number of prisoners are also being lodged in his brigade area. I think I can understand his alarm, that if his manpower is already stretched in his combat operations, to have a large number of prisoners he's got to guard as well, if they were to break out from where they were held would provide a real threat to his security. I can understand him being concerned. I also see he says: "All brigade forces are fully engaged and we have no reserves." This is quite a cry for help from the Commander of the Zvornik Brigade, who is particularly concerned about that large number of prisoners. I think those are the comments I'd offer on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, you've mentioned already -- you've actually already come on to it, but if you could shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 404/7, tab 30, when you mentioned reinforcements, and this is a document from the Krajina Corps Command dispatching an Infantry Company within that corps to the Zvornik area. What comments do you have about this document?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this document is, as you say -- and I just draw Your Honours' attention to the fact that it comes from the Krajina Corps, from a different corps, and it's signed by the Corps Commander, General Talic, at the bottom. It's clearly been in response, I would guess -- no, I don't guess, I notice it here on the screen -- pursuant to the document by the Main Staff. There's been a plea, if you like, from the Drina Corps to the Main Staff for reinforcements, and the Main Staff have ordered the 1st Krajina Corps to send a reserve formation across to the Drina Corps area to assist. And in response to that order from the Main Staff, General Talic from the Krajina Corps is ordering the commander of one of his subordinate brigades, the 16th Krajina Motorised Brigade, to prepare and dispatch an Infantry Company to the Zvornik area where it will be assigned to the Commander of the 1st Light Infantry Brigade. So this again shows to me that not only was the Drina Corps command chain working properly downwards, but it was also working upwards to the Main Staff to whom they sent a request for the reserves. The Main Staff had looked around the overall availability within the VRS at that time and looked to see that the Krajina Corps probably could afford to send some reserves and ordered them to do so, and they were now being -- and they were now being sent across. Paragraph 2 shows that the company is to be dispatched on the 16th of July by 2.00, by 1400 hours. It gives its direction of march and tells where it should go, to Zvornik, and to be there by the 16th of July by 2000 hours at the latest. So this underlines to me a fully functioning command and control system, and I expect, on a practical note, that the Commander of the Zvornik Brigade would be delighted to see the arrival of this company group from 1st Krajina Corps. It's only an aside issue, but the way that General Talic has written this order, that he wants this company that he's sending to be a well-organised, well-supported, and smart and efficient company in order to make sure that the Krajina Corps is shown off to be in a good light by those who receive it in the Drina Corps. This is all good military stuff and the sort of thing I would expect to see, and it shows the command and control system in the VRS working, and working well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, I just want to quote from your report at paragraph 58, page 18, and this concludes the questioning I wish to have in this area. "It is very clear to me that the whole operation was coordinated at corps level and that Major General Krstic, as Chief of Staff and later Corps Commander, would have been closely involved in the planning and execution of these operations." Can you comment any further on that statement that you make in your report? And this is specifically referring to the interception and mopping up of the column.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's probably already fairly clear from what I've said so far that with a number of major activities going on in the Drina Corps area, and when I spoke from the chart just now, I indicated the number of areas of the staff that would have been involved and the number of subordinate brigades that would have been involved in these operations, and there are several focuses or several areas of operation, the attack on Zepa; clearing up around Srebrenica; dealing with the column, particularly in the Zvornik area. There was a lot going on in the Drina Corps area. The issue of reserves underlines manpower was short. Request for manpower had been made to the Main Staff, and as I've just described, had been provided by the Krajina Corps. There is no way that this activity could have been conducted unless it had been coordinated and thoroughly organised and expedited other than through the Corps Headquarters. And this is the whole business and stuff of the Chief of Staff, to shift these various reports coming in, to understand them, and to make recommendations to his Commander about how operations should be developed. So to me, it is quite clear that in this fairly complex situation for the Drina Corps, there is no alternative other than the fact that the Corps Headquarters was fully informed as to the situation in these various areas, was taking decisions as far as these various areas were concerned, and that the whole activity in the Drina Corps zone of responsibility was a cohesive one being orchestrated quite properly and in the normal military manner by the Corps Headquarters, orchestrated by the Chief of Staff, keeping his Commander fully informed in the normal way. And it is what I would expect as a military commander, and it seems to me to be an efficient way of doing business, being properly delivered by the Drina Corps, and I recognise it as being a coherent and an effective piece of military activity going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Let me just ask you a puzzling question on that. Everything you've said has led to the conclusion, I think, that the Prosecutor's question indicated a coherent command system which people knew what their roles were and followed them, and yet you have as an overlay to this what happened. In other words, some place you had a massive violation of not only internal but, I suppose, international rules and everything. How can that happen in a coherent command system in which people have roles, they have communications going back and forth, everything seems fine in terms of the three operations going on simultaneously, but yet at the end of the line something completely out of range of normal military activity happens? I don't know if that's an answerable question but it keeps arising.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I've not been specifically asked about the detail about that, but I will offer a comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Just as a general proposition.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked about three activities going on, the attack on Zepa, the mopping up of the 28th Division column, and the movement of the civilian women and children. But of course there was this fourth activity going on, and implicitly I've referred to it in one of the exhibits we looked at a moment or two ago about the large number of prisoners in the Zvornik Brigade area. Where did they come from? Who were they? From other information I've seen, it seems absolutely clear to me that these are a number of the men who had been separated at Potocari and had been taken to schools in the Zvornik Brigade area, schools that I have visited. So what we have got here is an undercurrent chain of reporting. And because what was going on, as you've alluded to, ma'am, it contravenes and a lot of people knew this was contravening established norms and standards set down in the Geneva Conventions. It is not specifically mentioned in detail in these combat reports, because I think people wanted to keep that pretty quiet, but implicitly there are indications of what was going on. And I'm afraid my general point I have to extend and say that in the same way that the three legitimate operations were being properly coordinated, I can see no reason at all why that fourth operation was not being similarly and properly coordinated. That's a sort of dark implication I would have to draw from this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, was it possible to plan, to organise, and to execute all of these operations without the knowledge and without the participation of General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have to say that, because I go back, Your Honour, to one of my earlier points of yesterday, that command is a personal thing, and the commander must take and does take personal responsibility for all that goes on in his zone of responsibility. I know there is an issue that the Court has considered previously as to whether -- on what date General Krstic ceased being the Chief of Staff and on what date he became the Corps Commander, and I don't wish to address that. But I have made the point that those two appointments of Commander and Chief of Staff are unique in that they both have a responsibility to know what is going on. The Chief of Staff must gather all the information about all that is going on within the corps zone of responsibility in order that he can make the balancing decisions that I've just been referring to, balancing of the requirements of the three or four operations going on, and particularly when there are difficult issues. The minor ones he can take himself as Chief of Staff, minor decisions, but he must consult his commander to take major decision. I would expect, for example, the decision to ask the Main Staff for reinforcements from the Krajina Corps, I would be -- it's the sort of decision I, as a commander, would want to be consulted on before I went to the level above me to say, "I need reinforcements." So there are a number of things where the Chief of Staff undoubtedly would have to consult the Commander. And again it's a point I was making before and it's an absolutely critical one, that even if the Commander, whoever he was, had gone off to the forward command post at Zepa on the 13th, we've already seen that communications were is established by 6.00 on the 14th between the forward command post and the main command post so that information could still flow to the Commander. He may well have been focusing on the Zepa operation, but he can't distance himself and ignore what else is going on. It's too busy in his corps area to be able to say, "I'm just looking in that direction. You get on with the rest of it." It's a total responsibility, and the Commander and the Chief of Staff can't walk away from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another question. We are here talking about the 10th, 11th, 12th, 16th of July. You are a General with a great deal of experience. How is it possible to explain the substitution of General Zivanovic by General Krstic if such a substitution occurred, or replacement?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's a very good question. It seems hard to explain why you do not know why General Zivanovic was removed. There are a number of theories, and I don't know, so I won't comment on why General Zivanovic was removed. Undoubtedly, he was removed at some point and, undoubtedly, at some point General Krstic became the Commander. It will be most unusual to remove a Commander in the middle of an operation and most unusual to remove him in middle of a battle other than if he became a casualty. However, the operation to capture Srebrenica was undoubtedly completed 11th, 12th, in that sort of time frame, and the operation to move to and to try to capture Zepa was going to start 13th or 14th. Therefore, if I was going to change a Corps Commander, I would do it between those two principal operations. And given that General Krstic, as Chief of Staff, would have been principally responsible for the planning of the operation on Zepa, he was then very well-informed, very well-briefed, and very well-positioned to then become the Commander in order to command that operation. So to me, just looking at the practicality of it, once a decision had been made to remove General Zivanovic, the logical military time to put a new Commander in place would have been 13th, 14th, in order that the new Commander was there at the command post to lead the attack on Zepa. That is my military logical deduction. And I'm aware about funny dates and so on, but that's my military deductions in this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are talking about the good organisation, good communications, a military organisation that was functioning very well and that was well planned. So one could think that the evacuation of the population from Srebrenica was well planned and well thought out, so that they may reach territory controlled by the Muslim army. Why did the executions then occur? Do you have any idea, from the military standpoint, why such a plan occurred?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: If one applied a normal logic, Your Honour, it is difficult to see why executions on the scale that are -- that undoubtedly took place happened. I think one can only explain it by trying to dig into the unusual and rather bizarre logic that surrounds many events in the Balkans. I think we are deep into issues of ethnic tension and long-seated hatred which goes back over many centuries, and which had undoubtedly been found by the three or four years of the civil war. I think what I detect in here was a long-standing intention, and we see it from the political direction that I commented on yesterday, to capture Srebrenica and completely remove the Muslim population so that it could become a Serb town. But I think we see a late decision, having separated the men, then to kill them. And -- well, that has to be an evil decision, but I think it was a late decision. I think it was a decision based out of, sort of, vengeance, going back to deep-seated ethnic tensions. There is some pretty inflammatory language which one has seen being used on the video footage and in some of the transcripts, and I think that decision, which was a late decision, is not a military decision. It's one based on deep-seated history and hate, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can one say that this decision was outside the military officials, that it had escaped the attention of the military officials?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I can comment, Your Honour, on who took that decision. But once that decision had been taken, we're talking about operation, a black operation, if you like, a dark operation, which was conducted over a relatively short period of time. It was an operation of some magnitude which required considerable coordination of transport facilities to move people to holding areas, which themselves had to be identified and found; it involved identifying people who were able and willing to take part in the killing; it required other people with machinery to dig holes, to dig graves; it required other people to provide fuel for that equipment and fuel was in very short supply. So what I see is a dark operation going on, but one that was also a complex operation. That could not have been done other than by utilising the command and control structure which I've already shown that on the other operations was working perfectly effectively, and indeed from other bits of evidence I have been shown or I have asked to see, I see clear indications that fuel was being requested by the Drina Corps staff, that Engineer Units were being moved, and that the machinery of the Corps facilities were being engaged to conduct this dark operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: General Dannatt, before we go to another point, I would like to understand more clearly some of your very basic statements, whether in the report or right now. You spoke several times of the combat records. You spoke of the chain of command which worked properly upwards and downwards and the coordination which was extremely well done and vital, and you gave the example of the Zvornik Brigade and so on. All this covered the military aspect, apparently. Just for my knowledge, would you, as a General, be completely involved in the military aspect and be seriously involved and capable and leave the non-military thing as being irrelevant or even counter-productive and not be bothered with it? I mean, just the fact that you want to win the battles, let the soldiers go on killing, raping, whatever they do, what they do in wars, and if I exert more pressure on them, it might defeat my own purpose. So all this organisation, coordination which is the daily combat reports, which are called combat reports, are only concerned with the military aspect and let other things take their own course. Would you think that this applies to this very special situation in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, no, I don't think it does apply. I think the very nature of the VRS Corps, which, unlike my own division, the VRS Corps have zones of responsibility and that seems to give fairly comprehensive and total sort of responsibilities to the Corps, to the Commander, and to the Staff. And because these Corps are essentially local, they are quite well-integrated with the civilian authorities, and therefore although the prime focus of any military man in any military undertaking is to win the current battle that is going on, this whole background of other activities that are going on - the column, the civilians being moved, and so on - they all have to be seen in the overall context of the military operation. Because after all, we see the Drina Corps having to assemble a force to attack Zepa; that's going to require transport to move soldiers to the line of departure to start the attack on Zepa. But at the same time, we see 25.000 to 30.000 civilians being moved away from Potocari; that is going to require transport. Now, I don't think there was a limitless amount of transport. Somebody has to weigh up the requirements of the military operation and the civilian deportation operation and make a judgement and apply a priority: On this day, at this time, those 50 buses are to take part in the Zepa operation; on this day, at a later time, those 50 buses can be made available for the deportation operation. So while a military man is always going to be most interested on the combat operation, particularly in these circumstances, he's got to be aware of everything that is going on and balance up the priorities, balance up the availability of undoubtedly scarce resources, and fuel was very much a scarce resource, and make judgements. So I can't accept that it's possible for a military person just to focus on the combat bit and forget the rest. It's a complete spectrum of activities and events that will undoubtedly have to capture the Headquarters' and the Commander's attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You just said that you can't accept -- of course, I know you are a great professor of military tactics and so on, and you gave us this distinction between the Befehlstaktik which was applied in the JNA. Is your direction based on this idea that the JNA was a Befehlstaktik, where everything should be in the hands of the institutionalised commander, or is it on your direct observation?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's both, sir. The principle comes from central command and control and central, principally, top-down direction that undoubtedly is the doctrinal basis which I've observed from my theoretical studies. But from my own knowledge of operating in the Balkans and from the knowledge that I've gained in studying this operation, it's my deduction from the facts that I see that this was the process that was going on. I don't mean to labour the point about combat reports coming up and orders coming down, but this shows a very clear chain of information and chain of direction in place and being effectively used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Just another question before we go to another point. In your answer to the President, you seemed to indicate that the executions were decided at a late stage, the massacres and so on. I just saw in your report a statement where you said: "I have read the directive to the Drina Corps ..." and then you go on and say: "The document demonstrates that the siege of Srebrenica is being planned. Combat operations are to create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival for the inhabitants of Srebrenica." So do you think that was also decided at a late stage or it was a plan intentionally directed?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the intention from the extract which you've just quoted was to create such a situation in Srebrenica that not only would the town more easily be captured in a military sense, but that the people who had such a sense of fear and no hope of further life, that they would want to leave Srebrenica and go and live somewhere else so that it could become a Serb town. Now, I do not know and I'm offering purely a speculation. It could have been that a decision had been taken at an earlier stage to massacre a lot of the people. I do not know. It would seem to me that the intention was, by one means or another, to remove the people in a deportation sense so that it could become a Serb town and that the option remains open that the decision to separate the men and to kill them perhaps was taken at a later stage. But I will offer this as a speculative point on my part, and I probably should not make too strong a comment on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Well, you added, just in the same line: "There is a strong implication that where there is no territory, there is no life." You're saying they wanted Srebrenica without the people, and where there is no territory, there is no life. You were almost aware of the fact that there is no other territory for these people.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right, Your Honour. I mean, the people would have to go elsewhere to a Muslim area, and that is indeed what we saw, the deportation/transportation of the people. I think that was always the intention, that at the end of this operation, at the end of this period of time, that there would not be a Muslim population in Srebrenica, that there would be a Serb population in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You say: "... no life." "Where there is no territory, there is no life."

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: One can interpret that, really, either way. It could be "life" as in everyone having been killed or "no life" as in a community existence, a Muslim community continuing. No life, no living, no community existence, and that's, indeed, what we saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cayley, perhaps we can go on until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Between the three of you, you've actually covered much of the rest of my examination-in-chief. But I do have some other points to raise with the witness. In fact, there is one area that requires closed session but I'll do that after the break. I actually want to completely move to another area which I think will be of interest to the Court, and it is in respect of the intercepted radio communications. If Prosecutor's Exhibit 684 could be made ready for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, you're aware - you've seen some of them; you haven't seen all of them - that a large number of intercepted radio communications were acquired by the Office of the Prosecutor. These documents, the ones that I've shown you, show military traffic between a large number of different individuals both within the Drina Corps and the subordinate brigades and, indeed, the Main Staff, all these different units speaking to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If that exhibit could be placed next to the witness. This is simply one example.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, is this document discussing information of an operative nature?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this would appear to be a transcript of part of a conversation, and I see in the top line that there's reference to "They," the Muslims, "had close to 10.000 men of military age in Srebrenica," and "Have they reduced them by half?" is the other half of the conversation. "Yes, it must be close to half. 4.000 to 5.000 have certainly kicked the bucket," "kicked the bucket" being a euphemistic expression for having been killed. So there is information being discussed by these two people here about a large number of people of military age, 10.000, and about half of them, by one means or another, would appear to have been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, I don't wish to go through this whole document, but it does contain, other than this piece of information, a lot of information that appears to be of an operative nature of the activities of individuals within the Drina Corps, of NATO activities, and, really, it's a general question I have: Would individuals, in your opinion, speak about these kinds of matters, which one would believe to be confidential, on a line, on a military communication line that they knew could be intercepted and listened to by others?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military communications, Your Honour, ideally are conducted by secure means, that you can, therefore, have a private conversation from one person to another. Those secure communication means sometimes break down; sometimes the distances over which they've got to communicate make them inoperative, and, therefore, often people revert to what they know is an insecure means of communication. These days, increasingly mobile telephones are used or, indeed, the normal civilian infrastructure telephone network, a land line telephone network. Also, it's a feature of part of Bosnia and the Balkans that the land line telephone system often has a radio link, in part, and we know that some of the Serb-to-Serb communications were actually having to go through Muslim-held territory, and everyone would have known that. Therefore, people talking to one another, if they couldn't use a secure means of speech, may still have felt the need to talk and, therefore, would have talked knowing they were going to be doing so on an insecure means. Therefore, the way the military people try and get round this is to talk in, what we refer to as, veiled speech. You think you're hiding the meaning, but, in fact, when you actually analyse what is being said, it is pretty obvious. Now, an expression such as I've just referred to, "kick the bucket," that is not a very clever expression for people having been killed. But in other of the transcripts that I have seen, there is quite a lot of reference to people saying, "Don't say that. You know this is an open line," and I've seen another -- I've seen several where there are clear attempts being made to use veiled speech to hide what is being said knowing that others are listening. I'm afraid all armies do it. They shouldn't do it. But when you feel you do need to communicate and the insecure option is the only one available to you, then people go down that track, and it usually leads to a breach of operational security.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, General, I don't want you to make any comment on the reliability of all these documents, but based on what you've just said, do you believe it's quite possible that the Bosnian Muslim forces intercepted and, indeed, recorded a large number of conversations between VRS units within the Drina Corps area?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Undoubtedly. In the Balkans, everyone is listening to everybody else's communications. For example, the British Battalion at about this time in Gorazde, one of the other enclaves, knew that all its communications were being overheard, and because they are a Welsh battalion, they decided as a matter of policy to speak in Welsh, a language that no one can understand apart from themselves. It is a fact that everyone was overhearing everybody else, and therefore it doesn't surprise me in the slightest that there were these intercepts going on. I have to say that I think the quality of the intercepts are remarkably high. I have seen three different independent reports from three different interceptors of certain conversations, and the accuracy of what they've reported, I think, do indicate that they are accurate intercepts and informative as a result.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another question, please. General, as a General, you certainly have a great deal of experience and contacts with communications people, people doing their job. Is it possible for someone who is involved in a cause, to help its army to develop on the ground and in order to do that they need information, is it possible to envisage that somebody will trick others with misinformation or with something that he didn't actually hear, or vice versa? My question is: This information which was transmitted, do you think that it was really intercepted, or was it made up, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, your general point is a very fair one, and of course misinformation is very much something that people practice. The total amount of information and the total number of messages that are received have all got to be evaluated, and it's very much the responsibility of the Intelligence and Security Staff to analyse the massive information that comes in and to try and decide what is genuine and what has, perhaps, been artificially fed in. It's easy to feed in a piece of misinformation; it's quite difficult to feed it in in a consistent and coherent fashion that doesn't reveal the fact, after a period of time, that it's coming from an unauthorised source. With regard to the specifics here, as I've just commented, I'm amazed by the vast amount of intercept information that there is, that it comes from several different sources, several different people listening to the same number of conversations and producing what, to me, are pretty faithful and accurate reports of those conversations. So while I concede in principle it is possible for disinformation to be introduced, I believe that it's possible to spot disinformation from real information. In this case, the amount of good information is of such a high quality and consistency that I think that a fair degree of reliability, a high reliability can be placed on most of these transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, you have reviewed and read these intercepts of conversations on the one hand; on the other, you have seen orders and possibly conversations relating to those orders, and, as you have said, you have seen intercepts of the same sort of information but intercepted by different people. When you see this consistency of information, information captured by different people, is that information consistent or not? That is my first question. The second: Intercepts and what you read among the documents, orders, combat reports, and so on, is there a consistency there too?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: My short answer, Your Honour, is that there is a high degree of consistency. Now, inevitably there are some things that it's quite difficult to see exactly where they fit in, if it's only a part conversation or it's not entirely clear who was talking to whom. At what time is usually clear because that's actually fixed at a moment in time. But the remarkable thing is that given an order being passed -- let's say the order for the search operation issued on the 13th of July; I've seen transcripts of intercepts that relate to that kind of activity -- so there is a meshing in of one set of information with another set of information but, to a very high degree of consistency, does fit the various parts of the jigsaw together. When I was asked to help the Court by the Office of the Prosecutor, I had a general knowledge of what had gone on in Srebrenica overlayed on my own previous experience in the Balkans, but I have been amazed by the amount of information that is available on matters relating to this case and the degree with which pieces fit together. My own judgement is that it does give a high degree of reliability to many of the things that are before the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cayley --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It's four minutes past eleven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- have you finished with this point? Is it a good moment for a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I actually want to go into closed session for the next part of the witness' evidence, so it's probably a good moment to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We are going to have a half-hour break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The registrar tells me that we are in public session. So you may continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, I want to briefly and finally return to general principles of command and the particular concept that you spoke about early on in your testimony, that of command being a personal matter and of responsibility for everything that goes on within one's command. General, if a senior officer receives from his superior an order which is illegal, what should the subordinate officer do in those circumstances, in your view?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, in those circumstances, a subordinate officer obviously is in a difficult position, and he has a difficult choice to make between one or two courses of action. One course of action is to immediately remonstrate, to raise the issue with the superior officer who has given him the order that he believes is illegal, probably done privately, General to General, and to point out to him that the order he has given him is an illegal order and invite him to reconsider whether that is what he really wants to do. If that fails, then the junior officer, really, I think, has three choices: One is to comply with it on the basis that an order given by his superior is an order to be carried out even if he believes it's illegal and he doesn't like it; that's one end of the response spectrum. The other end of the response spectrum is, consistent with his view that it's an illegal order, to refuse to comply with it and in so doing to offer his resignation from his position as a subordinate general or a subordinate officer, remain true to his own conscience and resign his command and take whatever consequences there are. Or there is a central option, I suppose, that could be followed of knowing that what you've been asked to do is wrong, you carry it through on a minimalist basis. That, of course, is the worst, really, of all options because it's indicating that you know what you're doing is wrong. You're abdicating your responsibility, I think, to your subordinates and certainly abandon any pretense on being the moral high ground. So I think if confronted with an illegal order, there are those three responses that can be taken. In moral understanding and in international law, the only appropriate and reasonable course of action to follow is to refuse to follow the order which you've been given, and probably part and parcel of that is offer your resignation, if you haven't already been sacked by the superior, and take your chances within the structure that you find yourself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Just to complete your spectrum. You said being sacked. Is there something worse? Under the circumstances, in this very specific situation, was there something worse than being sacked?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. By "sacked," I mean dismissed. Of course, it's up to an army to decide what it will do with a general who refuses to obey orders. There are many examples in history whereby a general who refuses to obey orders is then shot. That, I think, is the far end of the spectrum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But in your experience, in this situation, was this a normal occurrence?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe I have come across an incident in the Balkans whereby a general who refused to follow orders has been shot. That's a sort of negative answer to that. I think there are cases of people being removed or dismissed from their position, which is quite common in military matters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You said: "I believe [sic] I have come across an incident in the Balkans whereby a general who refused to follow orders has been shot." Or has not been shot?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not been shot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Not.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Because they did not put "not." He has been shot. They have shot him here.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will clarify. I have not come across an incident myself in which a general who refused to follow orders has been shot. It may have happened; I've not come across it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Correct it on the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I've finished my examination-in-chief so I can offer the witness for cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Cayley. General Dannatt, you are now going to answer questions which Defence counsel will be putting to you. I see it is Mr. Petrusic who is going to cross-examine on behalf of the Defence. Mr. Petrusic, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, may I say good afternoon, Mr. President and Your Honours, my learned friends across the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the very beginning of this cross-examination, the Defence will start with Exhibits 425 and 426, please. Could I ask the usher for his assistance. General, I'm referring to Directive 7 and Directive 7/1. Could we have the other exhibit too, please, 426, provided to the witness.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have got both.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, looking at these two exhibits, these two directives and their contents, in terms of the objectives set to the Drina Corps, they are not identical. In Directive 7, issued by the then President of the Republic and the Supreme Commander, Radovan Karadzic, there is the sentence that says: "... through daily planned and well-thought-out combat activities create a situation of total insecurity and no prospect for the continued survival and life of the inhabitants of Srebrenica and Zepa." In Directive 7/1, issued by the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska - allow me to describe this as an objective - that objective laid down by President Karadzic is missing. My question is whether Directive 7, issued by the President of the Republic, is the basis for Directive 7/1, issued by the military leadership of Republika Srpska, that is, by the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand that question quite clearly, but I've been furnished with, I think, only the covering letter of 7/1 and I haven't got the substance of the order here. So before I can answer that question, I'm missing the second document in substance. Exhibit 426 is simply a four-line covering letter, and I haven't got the main document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, is it possible to do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, let me provide the witness with those documents. We have copies. The usher's assistance, please.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you don't mind, I'll just take a moment to look at this because I want to make sure I've got the right document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Take as much time as you need.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the reason I paused to take some time to look at this is because the obvious thing to do is to simply compare the piece in the first order relating to the Drina Corps with the piece in the second order just relating to the Drina Corps. If I just make that one direct comparison, in the second order, I don't see any reference to operations around Srebrenica which perhaps you would have expected to have been done given that in the order signed by President Karadzic it refers to Srebrenica. When I look at the orders in the second document, signed by General Mladic, first looking at the Drina Corps specifically, there was no reference at this stage to Srebrenica. However, I've looked at the general statement in the second order which comes first, which describes the overall conduct of the army's operations, and in that I see reference to operations to be conducted in the area of Srebrenica. The terminology about the survival or life of the inhabitants is not read across, but in the general statement of what the army is to do, it does indicate that operations should be mounted against Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So, General, only the military operation, the military operation known later on in the plans as Krivaja 95.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The normal military process is that when an order is written at a higher level, in this case we have at the highest level, an order written by the President, it's then passed down to the next level. In this case, the next level is the Main Staff of the army. They all receive the order from above; they all read it; they all analyse it. I call it a process which we term as mission analysis. You look closely at what it is you are required to do. You then conduct your own estimate of the situation, analyse the situation, think through all the various factors, and then make your own plan and express your own plan in your own operation order. What I see here is a high-level order received at the Main Staff level, analysed, thought about, a decision made, and then an operation order issued; and of course going down, that operation order, 7/1, is then issued to the subordinate corps, and we would see a similar order being thought about and then being produced at the Drina Corps level. So what I'm looking at is two parts of the process that started with the President and found it's way down to lower levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: If I understand the process correctly, the directive first reached the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska which then analysed that directive, and the directive of President Karadzic was used as a basis; then a new number was given to that directive based on President Karadzic's directive, and then the Main Staff issues to the Drina Corps this analysed directive for further analysis or, rather, for the preparation of operational plans for the implementation of the Operation Krivaja 95; am I right, General?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, if that is so, and you have just confirmed it, then the aim that President Karadzic spelled out in his directive to create unbearable conditions for life in Srebrenica and Zepa does not reach the Drina Corps and operational plans are not prepared at that level accordingly.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: If one is analysing the words, Your Honour, that are written down here, you're quite correct. I don't see a read across of the fairly colourful language used in the order signed by Mr. Karadzic. But as I've already said, what I do see in the Main Staff order is a reference to the fact that attacks will be developed towards the enclaves, including Srebrenica. As a military person, I would be very wary of including in my own operation orders the kind of language and the kind of intent that is actually written down in Mr. Karadzic's piece of paper. I perhaps would have an eye to the future. I would have an eye to what is proper, in military terms, and what is perhaps less proper, and I may well have carried the intent from the words written down at the political level, which is what effectively Mr. Karadzic has done. But I think I would be very wary of carrying that kind of language over into my military document. Although I, analysing Mr. Karadzic's order, would have understood what he had in mind, and I perhaps would have chosen not necessarily to have included that in the written part of my order. So I can see the point that the lawyer here is making, but I can understand why I don't see the same language being passed down from one document to another.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, in the operational documents that you had occasion to review in the course of your preparations for this testimony, the terms and concepts used by officers of the Drina Corps with reference to the attack on Srebrenica, were they proper in military terms? To be specific, regarding the order, the preparatory order for active combat activities, dated the 2nd of July, 1997, Exhibit 428, is it quite correct for the commander to say in his order, when he determines the objective of those operations on page 2, " ... by surprise attack to isolate the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa, improve the tactical position of forces deep into the zone, and create conditions for the elimination of those enclaves?"
