From the point of view of military terminology and military orders, is that a proper wording of a document of this kind?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the, Your Honour, overall military construct that I described earlier of deep, close, and rear operations, and deep operations being those things being done to give you a better chance of successfully carrying out your close operation, your close combat operation, then the language that I see here is consistent with that. In other words, by surprise, by artillery fire and shelling, that you would so reduce the will of the defenders to continue to defend. I see references in here, the task of carrying out offensive activities with three forces deep in the Drina Corps zone. These kind of deep activities are designed to be unsettling and to reduce the will of the defenders to continue to defend the enclaves of Zepa and Srebrenica, and that is the kind of language and kind of construct that I would expect. Now, that has a military derivation from the kind of language that the Karadzic signed piece of paper had, but interpreted into a more military fashion, and I, therefore, see a consistent thread from the political direction given by Mr. Karadzic, which is not there so obviously in the Main Staff order that I was taking some time to look at a moment or two ago. But the intention of that, I see carried across here in the Drina Corps operation to conduct those deep activities, those unsettling activities that are more likely to facilitate the successful outcome of the close operation, the actual attack on Srebrenica, so that it can be done quickly, decisively, and with minimal casualties to the attacking Serb forces. That is all pretty consistent, in my view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: General, let me ask you a question. In one of the earlier documents we saw the objective defined as keeping the enclaves within their original boundaries, preventing the free flow of various activities going on in between, all of which sort of are consistent with the status quo or what people thought the status quo should be. If you get an avowed objective to create conditions for the elimination of enclaves which have been set up for safe areas under an UN directive originally, do you run into a tension between correct military and lawful orders or objectives?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I can see what you're getting at, which I think is why the Karadzic directive is -- although the terminology is quite colourful, I think its worded something quite carefully because it doesn't actually specify that there will and deliberate attack to capture Srebrenica. It talks about creating the environment whereby life is unsustainable there, which would effectively have the same result. Going on beyond that, what I understand is that perhaps the overriding concern at the planning stage of this operation was not necessarily so much as the elimination and the capture of Srebrenica and Zepa, but to prevent the joining up by Muslim forces of Srebrenica and Zepa and, therefore, making an existing problem, in Serb eyes, worse. So I think part of the planning intention was to make sure they were kept apart. The stated hope of reducing them so the population left was, I believe, very much there. I think only subsequently, when the success of that was being evident, was the decision made to actually press home an attack and actually deliver the defeat of Srebrenica and, therefore, its subsequent evacuation by Muslims and availability to become a Serb town. I think throughout this, the Serb political level and higher military level had to keep an eye very much on international reaction here, and if they pushed too hard, they were always going to run the risk of an international backlash. As you, ma'am, quite rightly point out, these enclaves were subject to United Nations Security Council resolutions declaring them as safe areas, and if the Serbs pushed too hard against them, it is quite likely they might have triggered United Nations or NATO airstrikes against them. And I think to push slowly and gently and not inflame international opinion, that was probably the right way to go, and that is, as events turned out, exactly what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, according to your knowledge and according to the information and the documents that were available to you during this research, was the 28th Muslim Division concentrated in the protected area of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding, Your Honour is that the 28th Muslim Division was within the general enclave, geographic enclave of Srebrenica, not just in the town but in the rather larger area knocked out by the enclave. That was the location of 28th Division. Whatever, I have to say, 28th Division was. I don't think it's got quite as I would term it, joined-up a structure as the Drina Corps had.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Speaking of the members of the 28th Muslim Brigade, if they were the ones who were attacking or making incursions into the rear of the Serbian territory, Serbian-held territory, if they were attacking both the military and the civilian population, in that case, was the attack on the 28th Muslim Brigade a legitimate military objective, a legitimate military target?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just clarify that question? That you mean that the attack on the 28th Muslim Division, once it had broken out of Srebrenica and while it was trying to regain Muslim lines in the direction of Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Was the attack on the territory which was held on the 28th Muslim Division, that is, at the beginning of July 1995 and on the 6th of July, 1995, when the attack on the VRS actually began, at that moment, at that period of time, under the assumption that there had been attacks from the protected area and from the territory held by the 28th Muslim Division, was that division, at that time, a legitimate military target?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that. I understand the question. Within the enclave of Srebrenica there were Muslim forces which we know to be named 28th Muslim Division. Of course, under the terms of the United Nations Security Council Resolution that had declared Srebrenica to be a safe area, part and parcel of that Resolution was that military forces within Srebrenica should have been disarmed and not existed. Now, I think that's a separate issue which I don't want to comment on too much, which was the extent to which those Muslim forces had been disarmed by United Nations forces in Srebrenica. But I think we all know that there were a number of Muslim military men who were still bearing arms in there. The extent to which, therefore, the attack on Srebrenica was a legitimate military act, according to general Geneva Convention norms, is my answer is yes, it is not unreasonable for the Serbs to have attacked the enclave of Srebrenica in which there were known to be Muslim military men. That is a separate issue, in very general terms, to the more specific issue as to whether it was right for Serb forces to have attacked Srebrenica, which was itself an United Nations Security Council resolved safe area. That is a separate issue. And by terms of that United Nations Security Council Resolution, that attack was an illegitimate attack. It was against the Resolution of the Security Council. So I have two answers to that question for whatever value that adds to these matters before the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General Dannatt, in the division which is under your command, is there a principle of handover of control, of duty between two commanders, that is, between the outgoing commander and the incoming commander? Do you have that as an established principle in your division?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I hand over command of my division, I walk out of the door and get into my car and I drive away. The next day, my successor arrives and assumes command. There is not a process of time by which he and I work together and I hand over my responsibilities. That is the function of the staff. It's a bit like a monarchy, I suppose. The king is dead, long live the king. I finish my time in command, I go away, the next man arrives, he assumes command. It's the function of the staff to make sure that the incoming commander is brought up to speed with current issues. In terms of handover of command, there is not a period of time when we together. When I have in-staff positions, that is a different matter. One spends up to a week with the staff officer who is relieving you, going through the issues of substance to make sure that nothing falls between the gap. But the handover of command is what we would call a cliff-edge affair. I go; the new man arrives. It could be the same day; it could be a day or two later. But we do not have a practice in my army, at either battalion, brigade, or division level, and I've handed over command in all these different areas, where I spent time with my successor. I go away, the new man comes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So that happens at the level of the division and as regards the office of the commander of the division. Are you familiar with the regulations of the VRS to that effect, that is, is that procedure provided for in the same manner as in your army, that is, at the level of the commanders of the corps?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my study of the VRS regulations, I can't bring to mind a regulation that stipulates whether there should be a formal handover-takeover period between commanders at the corps level. I can't recall seeing anything to that effect. So I can only comment, I'm afraid, on what my own practice is, and not offer -- I'm afraid I cannot help the Court whether there is a regulation that specifies a handover-takeover period within the VRS. Actually, it's not the sort of normal thing in command terms because command is a personal thing. What my predecessor has done and what my successor will do are two different personal things, and I just refer back to the general principle that command is a personal thing. It's the staff that must keep the continuity of detail going. The tone, the trend, the principle is set by the commander, and to have a sort of clean end to your command and the clean start to the next chap is the most effective way of that delivering that personal command.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General Dannatt, while studying or, rather, while preparing yourself for your analysis, for your testimony, did you ever come across documents issued by the Drina Corps to certain units, such as brigades, after the 13th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I'm sure I have. I'm just trying to think. The 13th of July is obviously the date of Krivaja 95, the attack on Zepa; the 13th of July is also the date of the search operation which we spoke about earlier. I'm just trying to recall an operation order after that date. But amongst the many documents I've looked at, I'm sure I have seen one later but I can't immediately bring one to mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The documents or, rather, the regular combat reports coming from the Bratunac and Zvornik Brigades, were they addressed to the forward command post at Krivaca or to the command post or, rather, the headquarters of the Drina Corps in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, General. Just a second. Let me try to be more precise. I am referring to the 14th and the 15th of July.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I understand the question. I understood it originally as being, had I seen orders coming down from the Drina Corps. I understand the question to be, have I seen combat reports coming up from the subordinate brigades to the Drina Corps, and the answer is yes, I have seen those. I'm now trying to remember whether they were addressed to the forward command post or the main Corps Command. If I say I can't remember, in my own view, I don't think it really matters. I've already commented on the fact that the forward command post had communications established to the main command post from 6.00 on the 14th of July, and therefore, if the reports had gone to the forward command post or the main command post, the information was equally available at both those headquarters. Now, the usual way for a routine situation report to be passed is to go to the main headquarters. That is where, as I've already indicated on several occasions, the majority of the staff are, where the Chief of Staff probably is most usually, and that is where the information is collated. Important information is then passed across to the tactical command post, the forward command post. But to my mind, whether it's gone to one or the other isn't really an issue for me. The fact of the matter is both headquarters are in touch with each other, and information of any significance would be passed routinely from the main headquarters to the tactical headquarters for the information of the commander. After all, there is no point in having information if decision-makers don't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I will follow up on what you have just said. General, on the 14th and the 15th of July, at the Vlasenica command post, there is evidence about the presence of General Zivanovic at that command post. Was that of any relevance?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, we touched earlier on, I think it was this morning or was it yesterday, on the departure of General Zivanovic. When he actually disappeared is quite difficult to pin down. I see no evidence in any of the orders, reports, or intercepts of any reference to General Zivanovic after the 15th. In fact, from the 16th onwards he seems to have sort of dropped into a hole; he doesn't seem to appear at all. The only period of confusion in my own mind is the 13th, 14th, 15th as to whether General Zivanovic was still the Corps Commander up until the end of the 15th or whether, indeed, General Krstic had become the Corps Commander as early as the 13th. I think I've indicated that, to me, logically General Krstic would have become Corps Commander in time to properly conduct the Zepa operation which started late 13th, early 14th. It may well be that to do that, certainly for part of the time he was at the forward command post which had moved to Krivaca. Whether General Zivanovic was still, shall I say, hanging around the main command post in Vlasenica, I'm not sure. I've seen a couple of intercepts to indicate that he was there. I've seen one that said, "I'm packing my bags." I think that was on the 14th or the 15th. So it was quite clear that he was leaving. I've seen another one that says -- I think it was on the 15th, someone had asked him a question and he said, "Actually, I can't help you anymore," indicating that he had given up executive authority. So there is a little bit of doubt as to what General Zivanovic's function was on the 14th and 15th, but certainly from the 16th onwards, he appears to be irrelevant to the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Likewise, General Dannatt, since you've mentioned the conversations, we have an example of a conversation in which a lower-level officer was waiting for General Zivanovic upon his order, and also we have General Zivanovic addressing this lower-level officer, telling him, "You have to understand this as an order." So my question in relation to that would be: Was there, of any relevance -- was the presence of General Zivanovic at the command post on the 14th and the 15th of July of any influence as regards the situation, bearing in mind the various combat reports that are coming from subordinate units at that time?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I say again, I think General Zivanovic's position on the 14th and 15th is unclear. Whether he was or believed he was still the Corps Commander, I don't know. But what undoubtedly is a fact is that he was still a General on the 14th and the 15th and he had been the Corps Commander prior to that. So, undoubtedly, whether he still was or was not the Corps Commander, he still had some authority because he was a General and he carried over some authority in some respect because he had been the Corps Commander. Therefore, I'm not entirely surprised that he's still giving some direction. The Defence lawyer made reference to the fact of one communication where General Zivanovic says, "You are to take this as an order." Well, from those words, I would deduce that if he was still the Commander, he would have said, "You are to do this. You are to do that." Perhaps because he's no longer the Commander, he has to say, "You are to take this as an order." In other words, he realises that he is actually no longer in a position to give orders, but because he's a General and carries the authority of his rank, he is saying to some subordinate, "You are to take this as an order," "as if I was still the Commander." I hope I've made a distinction there that's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may ask a question. General Dannatt, if he had not been the Commander but only a General, would it still have been possible for him to say, "Take this as an order"?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's quite possible that he could have done that because he was a General and therefore more senior by rank to most other people who were around. What I have to say, as a military person, I find this whole business quite extraordinary, that there is doubt as to who was and who wasn't the Corps Commander in a combat situation. In driving a car, you can only have one person behind the wheel at any one time. Now, either General Krstic was the Corps Commander or General Zivanovic was the Corps Commander, and when I stand back from muddle of dates, and we've got the 20th and 21st being talked about, when I stand back from it, I come back to the answer and the analysis that I gave earlier: that the logical time for there to have been a de facto, in effect, change of command was between the end of the Srebrenica operation and the start of the Zepa operation; therefore, the 13th would seem to be the time that General Krstic effectively became the Corps Commander because that was the start of the new operation. I know that the order from Mr. Karadzic came later; I know that there was a handover of duty, a sort of party on the 20th and 21st. Well, it doesn't surprise me that that came later because organising people to come to a ceremony takes a little time. But the effective handover, to me, logically, was on the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, the then President, Mr. Karadzic, was the only person who had the authority to appoint the Corps Commander. Are you familiar with that regulation?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read that regulation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So in an organised army, as you have described the VRS -- strike that. In your division, speaking of your army, is it possible for a commander to be appointed by someone else except for the person who is empowered by law to appoint him as a commander?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: In practice, Your Honour, yes, this can happen. I will give you an example from my time as a Battalion Commander. My adjutant, my Chief of Staff --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, I'm sorry to interrupt you, but I'm speaking about the level of a corps or, rather, a division, and the appointment of a division commander in your army.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. Your Honour, I'll give you a different example in that case. At divisional level, in my divisional headquarters currently, there is the Chief of Staff of one of my brigades. It's integral to the divisional headquarters. This officer was not performing satisfactorily, and ten days ago I removed him from his post as Chief of Staff of the Reconnaissance Brigade. I did that because it was the right thing to do. However, the official posting authority is another officer called the Military Secretary who issues the written orders for the removal of someone and the replacement of someone else. That subsequently had to happen and took a number of days afterwards for the action that I had taken to be authorised and approved and for a replacement to be posted in. I took the action to remove the officer that I felt needed to be removed on my own authority, and I sought formal authority subsequently. Sometimes you have to do things slightly outside the regulations, trusting your own judgement. I did that ten days ago. I believe probably General Mladic did it on the 13th of July, feeling that General Zivanovic was not the correct officer to lead the attack on Zepa, that General Krstic was, and he subsequently sought authority from Mr. Karadzic to approve it. It was a risk, I guess, that General Mladic took.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me, General Dannatt. In the example you gave about you taking a decision and then being corroborated, suppose it was rejected. Weren't you running a risk?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So that was not -- I mean, you took it at your own risk.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used my judgement and exercised my own personal decision-making process, believing that what I was doing was right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: It was strictly on an official basis -- not you, but I mean it would not have happened.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I had gone by the book, I would not have acted in that way. But I think it's true to say, if you do everything absolutely by the book, you don't necessarily always make the best decisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: As far as General Krstic was concerned, was he the choice of Mladic or of Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have said, but I do not know, Your Honour, that he was the choice of General Mladic, the military Commander who knew General Krstic well; that he wanted him to command the attack on Zepa and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Because we had a speech by Karadzic praising very much General Krstic and saying that he could almost be as good as Mladic.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's very fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: That's a speech we have.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I have seen that, Your Honour. I believe that in professional military terms, I believe that General Krstic had a fine reputation and was, indeed, praised by Mr. Karadzic. Therefore, that does not surprise me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So that does not lead to a conflict between him and Mladic?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Maybe we're misunderstanding each other, sir. I said that I believe it was General Mladic's decision on the ground, if you like, to appoint General Krstic on the 13th of July to be the Commander of the Drina Corps so that he was there in the Command appointment before the attack on Zepa properly began, and it was subsequently approved by Mr. Karadzic. But as you, Your Honour, point out, Mr. Karadzic, quite clearly, had a high opinion of General Krstic from the speech that you've just referred to, and therefore, General Mladic would probably have known that he was not running much of a risk by himself appointing General Krstic, knowing that Mr. Karadzic would, in all probability, subsequently approve that appointment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: With the result that Mladic and Krstic were almost on the same wavelength.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suspect at that time, sir, they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, before the break - I apologise, Mr. Petrusic, I have to interrupt with a question - if General Zivanovic was not in a good health condition, for example, would you say the same thing, or would that change or affect your opinion in any way?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, if General Zivanovic was not in good health, then the automatic thing to have happened would have been for General Krstic to have become the Corps Commander, because as the previous Chief of Staff, by regulation, he was the Deputy Commander. So if the former Commander is no longer available through ill-health, then, by regulation, General Krstic would automatically have become the Commander. As I said before, I do not know why General Zivanovic was removed, whether it was health or whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but in that case, we could have General Krstic replace General Zivanovic and then afterwards there would be a formal appointment; am I correct in understanding you?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If, let's say, General Zivanovic had been unwell for a period of time, then quite naturally General Krstic would have exercised the function of Corps Commander until General Zivanovic had got better. That would have not required an order from Mr. Karadzic. The regulations provided for General Krstic to be in the Command appointment. However, General Zivanovic did not come back so, therefore, I deduce that he was not replaced as a result of ill-health; he was replaced for some other reason. And my earlier comments, I think, are the comments that apply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, would this be a convenient time for a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. We will have a 45-minute break, and I still hope that we won't have to work until 3.30. A 45-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, you may now continue, but please bear in mind that we have to make some effort and try to finish by 3.00, and only if it is necessary we will work until half past three, in which case, we will have a short break for the benefit of General Krstic. If we have to make a break, it will be a 15-minute break only.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I do hope that we will be able to finish by that time and that we won't have to have a break, but this also depends on the General and his answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General Dannatt, let us briefly deal with the following issue. We spoke about President Karadzic and General Mladic at some length, and I should like to know whether you know what kind of relations they had as regards the issue of commanding; that is, what is the relationship between him as the Commander in Commander of Staff or the Supreme Commander and the Commander of the Main Staff? What were the relations at the time? Were they, so to speak, adequate?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, as much as I'd like to help the Court, I really don't think I can offer a useful comment on that particular topic. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge as to the fact that at the beginning of August 1995, President Karadzic attempted to replace General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was, I think, a matter that was quite widely reported, and I'm aware of that in general terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me. Can I just ask you a speculative question in this line? Could General Mladic have been able to interfere and stop the nomination of General Krstic had he wanted it?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, you asked me to speculate. My answer is a speculation. I believe that had General Mladic not been content, had not been approving of the appointment of General Krstic as Corps Commander, I think he certainly would have said so to Mr. Karadzic, and indeed I think it's also quite possible that Mr. Karadzic may well have discussed with General Mladic his intention to appoint General Krstic as Corps Commander. Raising the issue to one of generality, certainly within my country, within my army, the most senior appointments are recommended by the senior military for approval by the political heads and there is some discussion that goes on. So both the Chief of the General Staff, the Chief of the Defence Staff and the Secretary of State for Defence in my country both have to agree that a particular person would have a position of appointment of such seniority as a corps commander. That's a general answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, on the assumption that Mladic appointed Krstic as a Corps Commander on the 13th of July, that is, are we speaking on the basis of an assumption that Mladic appointed Krstic as a Corps Commander on that date? Is it your assumption that this was done by Mladic?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's my military opinion that logically, the sensible time to have changed the command of the corps would have been between the Srebrenica operation and the Zepa operation, and, therefore, the date of the 13th of July would seem to be the most sensible. And my speculation is that this was a military decision, and that General Mladic probably made that decision and then sought, subsequently, approval from Mr. Karadzic. That is my military view, with some speculation added to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you think that the chief of staff of a corps can take over the command duty over the corps only in the absence of the commander or in cases of his unavailability or in case that he is prevented from fulfilling that duty for any reason?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The regulations are quite clear that the general officer who holds the appointment of chief of staff is also the deputy commander, and he would exercise the command function in the absence for whatever reason, injury, illness, leave, of the appointed commander. Yes, that is a normal -- that is what the regulations provide for.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, apart from an order for active combat operations in respect of Srebrenica, do we have any other well thought out plan for the implementation for the Directive 7/1? I think that the Exhibit in question, 426, has been widely used. I don't think it is necessary for putting it on the ELMO once again. So except for that particular order, do we have anything else, any other specific document concerning the Directive 7/1?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just reflecting for a moment to see what I can remember. Your Honour, I believe part of the answer to the question is that the overall directive, which came from Mr. Karadzic, that then produced the Directive 7/1, which was the order for the attack on Srebrenica, it was same Karadzic-level produced document that provided the background for the subsequent operation order for the attack on Zepa, Krivaja 95. So I think the Karadzic-level document provided the higher-level instruction for both of those. So the answer to the question is yes, there is a second operation order, and that's the Krivaja 95 operation order.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I see in the transcript "Zepa" in relation to the Krivaja 95 plan. I believe it's a mistake because the Krivaja 95 plan actually concerns Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm referring to the two separate operation orders, the one for the attack on Srebrenica and the one for the attack on Zepa subsequently, the one issued on the 13th of July, which was signed by General Krstic as Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic -- Mr. President, Excuse me. I don't want to interrupt my learned friend because we want to move quickly. But I do believe that if Defence counsel is making reference to documents, the purpose of the cross-examination is not to conduct a memory test on the General as to what he can remember. It would be better if he actually puts the documents in front of him because that would, I think, probably speed things up and make it easier for the General to remember rather than him having to remember the thousands of documents' specific content. It's just an observation I make. It's not an objection as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I think you're right, Mr. Cayley. But I believe that Mr. Petrusic was trying to obtain the same result without the actual use of documents. But in any case, it is much better to have the General see the document so that he can remember things. I think it is an easier way to proceed. There is always a risk, when we want to act in a speedy manner. So, Mr. Petrusic, it perhaps would be better if you ask the registrar to have the document be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I believe that the witness has answered my question, so we don't believe there is any need to go back to the document and have it placed before the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Petrusic. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, in your analysis, you stated that you were not surprised by the presence of Mladic and Gvero, that is, the Commander of the Main Staff and his assistant, and that as regards the structure of a military command, it is a usual practice for the higher command to follow carefully the main effort, the main events. In relation to that and bearing in mind your experience in Bosnia and Herzegovina, how do you interpret the fact that the superior officers were actively following duties of their subordinate officers but that they did not have enough scope, enough room for action and decision-making process without necessarily involving even higher military levels? How do you interpret that within the framework of the actual developments of the actual situation in the area of Srebrenica after the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just making sure, Your Honour, that I follow the exact line of the question. I think, Your Honour, I rather disagree with the premise of the question. What I have said hitherto is that the presence of General Mladic and some of his assistants, some of his staff in the area of the Drina Corps, I don't find surprising because that's where the main effort for the VRS at that time was. Because General Mladic was there, I would expect him, quite properly and quite normally, to have endeavoured to influence events. After all, he was superior by appointment and rank to, we'll say, General Krstic, to the Corps Commander at the time, and, therefore, could well have given additional orders and sometimes additional advice. There is a difference between the two. "You are to do this," "I suggest you do that," but it's all done following the structure of Mladic to Krstic and using the organ of the Drina Corps to carry out those commands. The bit of the question that I don't follow is the implication that's between General Mladic on the Main Staff level and General Krstic and his Drina Corps level, there was a requirement to go apparently higher to seek authority for a number of these sort of things. I don't see any evidence that that happened. I think that from my understanding of events that took place leading up to the capture of Srebrenica and that which followed after the fall of Srebrenica, they were issues that were decided by the Generals on the ground at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me. "Between the Generals"? I thought there was one General.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm trying to address the issue of the fact that General Mladic was also present in the area of Srebrenica at the time and the fact that he undoubtedly would have had conversations; he may have given orders to General Krstic. So I use the term "Generals," plural; General Mladic and General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And how would that interfere with the responsibility?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wouldn't at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Then who would be responsible in that case?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The normal passage of formal orders is as we've been describing over the last couple of days, of issuing a formal operation order from one level to another. But it's perfectly proper for the Superior Commander, in this case, General Mladic, to give additional orders or additional instructions to General Krstic as Corps Commander, face to face, in a spoken way, at the time, telling him to do this or to do that. Then one would expect General Krstic then to issue instructions to his own people within his Corps to carry out those instructions. This is the way that I would normally understand the senior commander being present to influence the conduct of operations in a given area, the key area of the main effort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But there was no sign of General Mladic giving direct orders to the subordinates of General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I think we've looked at that several times previously, and I can see no evidence of General Mladic giving direct orders to constituent parts of the Drina Corps and, therefore, bypassing the normal Corps command and control structure. I don't see any evidence of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, if we are talking on the basis of the assumption that oral orders are also being issued, as you yourself have just mentioned, by General Mladic in this case, in the period of the 11th, the 12th, and the 13th of July, when General Krstic was the Chief of Staff, would it be natural or logical for General Mladic to issue such orders to the Corps Commander and not to the Chief of Staff of the Corps?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the normal and correct way of doing business would be for General Mladic, if he felt it appropriate to issue some additional or fresh orders, to do it to the Corps Commander, that is, the strict chain of command. I think, however, having made quite a lot of, over the last couple of days, the unique position of the Corps Chief of Staff as the principal staff officer, also a general officer, that it would not be wrong for General Mladic to issue orders to the Corps Chief of Staff, in the clear expectation that the Chief of Staff would immediately inform his Corps Commander that he had been given those fresh orders. It's quite usual, in my experience, for orders to be given and received by a commander to a subordinate chief of staff in the expectation that there is an immediate discussion between the chief of staff and his appropriate commander. Strictly, orders would go commander to commander. But given the particular nature of the Chief of Staff position, and he was a General, I don't find it particularly unusual - and we are talking in terms of hypothesis here - that General Mladic might have given some orders to General Krstic who could well have been still the Chief of Staff at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: As regards the regulations which were applicable within the VRS; namely, the regulations which had been adopted from the former JNA, in accordance with those regulations, does the corps commander issue orders to his assistants?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I just clarify, Your Honour, what Defence counsel means by "assistants"? Does he mean assistant commander as per that diagram or does he mean subordinates as in brigade commanders?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The corps commander has his assistants for morale, religious issues, for logistics and for security, so I'm referring to those assistants.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for clarifying that. It would be perfectly normal for the corps commander to issue instructions to his assistants responsible for those functional areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: A corps commander also issues orders to his subordinate units such as brigades or, rather, to the commanders of those brigades.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, during the time that you spent working on this case, did you ever learn that the first documents relating to the transport, the evacuation or, if I can use the term from the indictment, the deportation of the population from Potocari, are such documents related to the date of the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, I'm sorry to interrupt you, but I think it would be useful to see the documents. Otherwise, we will be testing the General's memory which I trust is very good; however, it should not be tested here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, of course. If you can just give me a moment. I will withdraw this question for the time being. But I should like the assistance of the usher to put Exhibit 459 on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, this information comes from Colonel Jankovic, and it was issued from the forward command post in Bratunac on the 13th of July, 1995. General, could you please tell us - you have already spoken about the subject this morning - why Colonel Jankovic, who is an intelligence officer of the Main Staff, is transmitting this to the Intelligence Sector of the Main Staff and to the Command of the Drina Corps and its Intelligence Department? Why is he transmitting this piece of information to these two addressees?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I assume that he is doing that because he has been in the area of operations covered by this report, probably in the company of General Mladic, and he will have seen things going on, he will have seen events going on, and felt it appropriate to pass on that information, in the same nature of the dialogue between one intelligence officer to another, to the Command of the Drina Corps so that it's accurately and properly recorded. After all, we're dealing with an army conscious of regulation, conscious of keeping good records, and by making a report like this, as one intelligence officer to another intelligence officer, it was a way of ensuring that the information was properly recorded and found its way into the framework and network of information-gathering that the Drina Corps, which had the geographic responsibility for that part of Republika Srpska -- was properly documented and recorded. I can see what Defence counsel is alluding to here, but I don't see anything particularly unusual about it. It's exactly the same example we discussed this morning of not the command relationship but the information relationship between one headquarters and another.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Assistant Commander for Security in the Corps, is he in charge of controlling the Security Organs in a professional way?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, he is responsible for coordinating all the people that work in the security and intelligence area in the same way that the other branch heads in the functional areas are responsible for their functional areas. But they are part of the Corps Headquarters structure and, therefore, are answerable to the Chief of Staff, and then on upwards to the Corps Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: From your research, do you think that this is the only responsibility, the only duty? As regards the hierarchical structure, is it going upwards to the Corps Commander, or, bearing in mind the nature of the work that they do, do they also have a responsibility in respect of the Intelligence and Security Organ of a higher command; in this case, it would be the Security Organ of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general terms, the responsibility within the security and intelligence area is the same as the responsibilities for any functional area. I can imagine, perhaps, some circumstances where there was some information of a very sensitive nature that was kept within the intelligence community, but that is usually for the purpose of the protection of the source of that information and is never intended to be denied to the commander. Indeed, in my own experience, on operations when I've fulfilled the post of Commander British Forces, I have had intelligence officers who have come to brief me personally on relatively sensitive bits of information that aren't more generally known within the staff, and this is to invariably make sure that the source, where this information has come from, has remained privileged and protected and can continue to be used. But in general terms, the intelligence function operates in the same way as the operations or the transport or the logistics function.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Again, the Intelligence Service, did it have its special rules and regulations of service?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware, it has, within the overall regulations, some detailed provisions and requirements in the same way that all the functional areas have some detailed regulations and requirements laying down how they should do their business.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Let me now go back to the question involving Exhibit number 437. General, if there was a plan to conduct a deportation, such a document or a document similar to that document, would it have to be transmitted prior to that date?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just want to look at the transcript of your question to make sure I understand it correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: For the record, would such a document have been issued prior to the 12th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, if I understand the question correctly, we're trying to examine as to whether the deportation was a previously planned event or whether it was the result of a late decision. I think it's quite difficult for me to speculate on that. All I can say, from various reports and documents that I have seen, is that undoubtedly there was an urgent request placed for buses and trucks to remove people. I can't remember whether I have seen any such requests that date before the 12th of July, but certainty the Exhibit 437, which we were discussing a moment ago, is dated the 12th of July, and that is one of many documents related to the requisitioning and gathering together of transport. But I think I've already expressed the view that although there was intention to apply pressure to Srebrenica and the long-held aspiration to capture it, it was something of a surprise, I think, to the Serb military authorities to find that the United Nations, the International Community were not responding to the beginnings of their attack on Srebrenica. So, therefore, it was a relatively late decision to press home the attack and actually capture the town and, therefore, start the process that led to the deportation of the people. If that presumption is correct, it is, therefore, no surprise to me that the gathering together of transport was something that was done in rather a hurry and in rather a short time frame. So what I'm really saying is, I don't believe the intention to gather together transport and the intention to deport the people was a decision taken a long time in advance. It was consequent upon other things happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General Dannatt, would the use of transport means be part of the functions of the Rear, the Logistics Services and the Transportation Services?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the transport is one of the branches of the Department for Rear Services shown on the left-hand side of that diagram under the Department for Rear Services. Yes, it's one of the functions of that part of the Corps Headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: To the very end, General Dannatt, it is not my intention to test your memory. I simply do not have at my disposal those exhibits. But while preparing for your testimony, did you note, in the area of Zepa and within the framework of another operation that was conducted from the 13th and 14th of July, did you note the presence of Intelligence Organs, Intelligence and Security Organs in that area if you had access to any such materials in the course of your study?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid, Your Honour, I can't help you with that question. I understand the question, but I've got no information to give you by way of an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General Dannatt, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Mr. President. That ends my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Petrusic. Mr. Cayley, any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Very quickly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the witness could be provided with Exhibit 425, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: General, if could I refresh your memory to the beginning of your cross-examination when you were examined on whether or not the substance of Directive 7/1, and rather, I think you called it inflammatory or flowery language contained in the document was contained in subsequent orders down through subordinate units. If I could direct you to page 14 of Exhibit 425, paragraph 6.1, and it is the third paragraph from the bottom of that page, and I will essentially summarise what the directive is, and essentially the document states that: "UNPROFOR and humanitarian organisations are to be restricted so that, in essence, logistical supply is strangled to the enclave both for UNPROFOR and resources to the Muslim population, essentially making them dependent upon the goodwill of the VRS." Now, the one simple question I have for you, General, is: Are you aware whether or not that actually happened on the ground at Srebrenica? Are you aware whether or not logistics were interfered with by the VRS and supplies were limited coming into the enclave?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm very much aware. The Dutch Battalion that was the UNPROFOR garrison experienced considerable, almost extreme difficulties in bringing supplies in. It got to the point where they didn't have sufficient fuel for their vehicles and had to start foot patrols. Their food was considerably reduced and, in fact, as a result of roadblocks and checkpoints that were placed on their access into Potocari and into Srebrenica, the effect described by this paragraph here was very much the effect that happened on the ground. And as you would imagine, if it was happening to the Dutch Battalion garrison of UNPROFOR, it was happening even more so to the Muslim population. And I think there was the same -- I know there was the same denial of UNHCR relief convoys into Srebrenica. So the intent to make life very difficult for the UNPROFOR garrison and for the Muslim population was very much carried out on the ground. There is no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you've been very clear, General, but in essence, this directive from the Supreme Command of the Armed Forces of the Republika Srpska was, in fact, carried out on the ground in Srebrenica by units far down the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no doubt about it because it would have been elements of the Drina Corps, more than one brigade that were manning the confrontation lines around Srebrenica, and the approach routes from the Muslim-held territory where the support bases for UNPROFOR were located. They would have all responded to this instruction and in an orchestrated fashion have inhibited the resupply process going to the UNPROFOR garrison and to the Muslim people. Indeed it was happening in Zepa and Gorazde as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President and Your Honours, I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Cayley. Judge Fouad Riad, do you have some more questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: General Dannatt, I would still like to have some precisions, although I have understood you very clearly. You spoke about of the daily combat reports, and I can just quote one part of your report. You say: "I have seen evidence of daily combat reports that are clearly in a layed-down format which provides a full account of all activity." Did this daily combat report give an account of the massacres?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I have not seen direct reports of what you would describe as massacres. As I said in an earlier answer, there were -- and I wouldn't expect to do so either, because I think most people would have realised that to commit to paper, in a formal daily report matters like that, was laying themselves open to subsequent investigation as indeed the business of this court is all about. But one does see in some places references to things that one knows afterwards were indirect references, whether it's to prisoners, and I'm thinking now of the Zvornik Brigade's report complaining, if you like, of the large number of prisoners being held in schools and other reports relating subsequently to engineer equipment being moved and fuel being requested or being made available. So I see no direct reference to what you've described, sir, as massacres, but I have seen several examples of indirect references that we now know refer in part to that process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, to go further, if these daily combat reports were submitted to the Higher Command, so the Higher Command was not informed about the executions if they are not mentioned in the combat reports. Just to follow the echelon. How would you know about it?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a direct sense, Your Honour, I agree with you and -- I would agree with that point, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But still it will -- he'll remain responsible?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly remains responsible, but there are two parts to this information exchange process, Your Honour. There are upward reporting of what is going on, but then of course there is the downward ordering of what should be done. The mere fact that in the daily written combat report we don't see reports of that aspect of activity being reported up does not necessarily mean, on the one hand, it wasn't happening, and on the other hand, that it hadn't been ordered from above. I think a sensible subordinate commander would not have included such material in his daily combat reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And a sensible commander would not order it in written documents also, vice versa?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he has an eye to the future and what might happen, I think that would also be the case, that you wouldn't issue written detailed orders ordering what we would regard as a crime and orders instructing something to happen that is known to be against the Geneva Convention and against common humanity. Those are the sort of things that are dealt with by spoken word. I certainly wouldn't write it down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And in a well-disciplined army, this should still be done within the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Instructions to do things should still follow the chain of command, as I've just tried to clarify, but I wouldn't expect to see that sort of thing written down. However, the sort of things that we're talking about are not the sort of activities that I would expect a civilised, disciplined army to actually do. There is no doubt that these dreadful things happened. They happened extensively and over a short period of time, and, therefore, I have to make the dreadful deduction, if you like, that for this widespread activity to happen over a short period of time, it had to be facilitated by a disciplined, joined-up organisation to make such activity happen so quickly, and there was no other framework to enable this to happen other than the framework of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, you spoke of a civilised army. In one of your -- apparently when you were describing the plan Krivaja 95, you said it has a fairly barbaric logic. So that's not very much in harmony with what you said about a civilised army.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the term, Your Honour, that I've used mostly as been "disciplined," as disciplined as in following a chain of command, downward instructions, upward reporting. I don't think I've used the term "civilised" very often, and if I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Right now you did, five minutes ago. I'm not blaming you, I'm just telling you.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm probably trying to clarify that there is a distinction, a sharp distinction, in my mind between "disciplined" and "organised" on the one hand and "civilised" on the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So why do you say it was a fairly barbaric plan, the plan Krivaja?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The intention to shell, the intention to make life unsupportable, the intention to make life unbearable for principally civilians has a barbaric logic, and I think that comes into the uncivilised category.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: It carried already the intention of harming people.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Going right back to the original document that we looked at earlier, going back to the Karadzic-signed document which talks about there being no hope for life and making survival difficult, if there's a barbaric logic to that, and that implicitly -- that implies harm and casualty and fear being created amongst not only military people but amongst civilian people, that is not certainly civilised behaviour either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You were discussing transportation and wondering why there were no written documents concerning it. Would you put this under the category of unwritten exchange of orders and documents?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: To clarify, Your Honour, I said that I could not recall any written documents relating to transportation before about the 12th of July. I have seen written documents requisitioning transport, organising transport, for the purpose of what we know now is deportation subsequent to the 12th. So I have seen elements of that written down, and I've also seen transcripts relating to that. Indeed, one of the documents I was shown, I think it was number 437, a few minutes ago was such a written order requesting 30 buses to go from one place to another. So I have seen written-down evidence of the gathering of buses for the obvious purpose of transportation of people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Fouad Riad. Madam Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: General Dannatt, I have three questions. The first is a bit complex but be reassured the second two are very simple.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I wonder if you would consider for a moment a slightly different scenario, hypothetical, for the moment, obviously, than the one discussed at length which was whether or not General Mladic might have gone in and taken direct command of certain units of the Drina Corps and exercised that command. We also discussed at a later point whether or not, and you agreed, a logical time for General Krstic to take over as Commander would be at the end of the Srebrenica military campaign, the beginning of the Zepa military campaign. And occasionally, a good commander-in-chief jumps the box a bit and faces the consequences. Joining those two thoughts together, I would just like your comment on the possibility of a scenario which went like this: General Mladic - wanting General Krstic to go and lead the Zepa campaign, knowing that he was slated to become the Commander, if you went by the Karadzic letter, effective July 15th, which was a few days henceforth - decided to jump the box, as it were, let him become Commander for the Zepa operation but continue General Zivanovic in his present Commander status for the mop-up operation down the line, in which case there wouldn't be a need to go over generally; they could work, as you put in your report, glove in hand. And General Zivanovic whom, for the moment hypothesise, might have been more sympathetic to the style of General Mladic, and together they could regulate the lower part while General Krstic went on the upper part? Is such a scenario feasible, or is it highly unlikely?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, it has to come into the highly unlikely category.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. You tell us why.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I'll tell you why. There can only be one commander in a military establishment at any one time. I think I alluded to one person behind the steering wheel of a car. It would flout all the norms of military conduct to have two commanders at any one time, and I think that's a generalisation but I think it's a pretty strong generalisation. Secondly, General Zivanovic has completely disappeared off --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Not until the 15th.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am, that's correct. We see no further transcripts or documents relating to General Zivanovic after the 15th, I would agree, but that mop-up operation was ongoing for some time; the search in the woods went on for several days. So I think that would defy that part of the hypothesis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: But some of the heaviest of the massacres had already finished by the 15th.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking of two or three things here, I think, if I can just clarify. We're mopping up the column, the 28th Division column; we are dealing with the search operation - I was going to come to that - that was ordered on the 13th; and we're also dealing with what I've referred to previously as "the dark operation," to massacre a lot of people. I would agree, in the main, the killing was largely over on the 15th but it did run to an extent on the 16th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the burial aspect went on beyond, and of course the digging up and reburial was well beyond. So even if General Zivanovic had been the driving force behind that to start with, he very quickly stopped being so in that hypothesis and someone else, very early on, took it over. I would just come back to the other point which is the search operation, which was definitely not being ordered in the Zepa operation which was ordered on the 13th of July, and an order that was signed by General Krstic. So for all those reasons, I can understand how one could arrive at that hypothesis, but I would put it into the highly unlikely category for the three or four reasons that I have just given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. The two shorter questions. If you, as the commander of a corps or a division, suddenly found yourself in a combat situation which you hadn't anticipated - what I'm talking about is they might not have found out about the column marching towards Tuzla until the morning of the 12th, et cetera - but you then realise that you have on your hands some kind of a potential military operation; if you also anticipated that that might well result in taking a sizable number of prisoners of war in it and you wanted to handle them according to international law, et cetera, what kind of preparations, even if they were last-minute, would you expect the authorities to have to take if they were really going to treat people who were captured as prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they're going to do it properly, then first of all a body of troops, a unit of some sort, has got to be appointed to act as a guard force for that. I mean, it might be that you would choose a military police unit or it might be that you select an infantry battalion to be a guard force to prevent those people from escaping. You would have to identify places that you were going to hold those people. That might be buildings that you would be required to identify which were large enough, warehouses or factories or anything like that, to put people in, in other words, provide accommodation for them, or alternatively you would have to build pens very rapidly with wire stockades and so on in which to put them. You would then, knowing that you were dealing with large numbers, have to make some arrangements for the provision of food and water for the sustainment of those people and, on the presumption that these people were being taken prisoner after a period of combat, then provide medical services to at least give basic medical treatment; according to the Geneva Convention, at least as good as that which you would provide for our own people to sustain those prisoners. So there are quite a lot of activities that you would have to put in place, and that would require a degree of planning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Would it require that those holding places have enough food, medical care for a period of time? You mentioned that all during this war, the Bosnian war, there were these kinds of exchanges that went on between the BiH army and the Bosnian Serbs, exchanges of prisoners, so I assume this would not be an entirely new situation. But would you have to assume that you might have to hold those prisoners for a period of time before such an exchange was -- in other words, it couldn't be done overnight.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's absolutely right. Exchanges take a little while to organise. One's got to get in touch either directly with the other side or, as was often done, through the International Committee of the Red Cross, who acted as the intermediary in order to facilitate exchanges. That would certainly have taken a period of days; it may have taken a period of weeks. Of course, this is going beyond a little bit, but if they had taken 4.000 or 5.000 prisoners at this stage in the war, exchange was one option, but continuing to detain them for a longer period of time might have been a better option rather than put 4.000 or 5.000 potentially back in uniform as rearmed soldiers to fight against them once more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: My last question. You said, I think I quote you accurately, that it was your opinion, or at least your speculation that the decision to execute the prisoners was probably made late. I think you used the word "late." Can you tell us, knowing everything you know about the situation here, how late in this course of events could that decision have been made? I mean, in other words, did it have to be made before the buses left Potocari? Could it have been made after the buses left Potocari and the time the first groups of prisoners began to be assembled from the column? Given what we know here, how late in the game could that decision have been made?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the people, as I understand it, Your Honour, who were massacred came from two sources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some were prisoners captured from the column --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: The majority, yes.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and some were men from Potocari who were separated out from the women.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess that the decision to kill probably stemmed from the Potocari separation exercise and then carried on as a response to a number of those who were captured as the column was rounded up. So after all that, that took place over a number of days, and it was quite some time before the last elements of the column had been rounded up. So I believe that the decision to kill the men was a decision taken in the Potocari environment and then, to an extent, it was rolled across to a number of the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Although, weren't some of the first executions of the column people done on the 13th whereas the Potocari people were bused and held around Bratunac before some of them were then dispersed to camps and killed? That doesn't mean your answer can't be correct that the decision was made but ...

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, actually, some of the killings of prisoners from the column may well have come into the spontaneous category. I think that we may well have had a little revenge-taking going on there, and that may have been a less-disciplined aspect of the whole thing. I think the more sinister aspect of this is the major decision that was taken to separate men from women and children and then to execute the men, and that originally stems from the large group of people rounded up in Potocari. I agree with your difference over the dates there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I also have a few questions. My first question is the following: You said that it was normal for General Mladic to be present in the field of operations and that he could give instructions or orders of an additional nature. I think that you saw the video recording of the meetings held in the Fontana Hotel. The fact that we saw Mladic alone conducting the negotiations - Krstic did not speak; the other officers did not speak - how do you view that situation? It would have been normal for Krstic or Zivanovic to be able to speak and not for Mladic. He was there just to support them.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, two or three comments there, if I may. I presume that in advance of those meetings that were filmed and we've seen on the video, that the Serb Generals would have had a meeting beforehand and decided what they were going to do. I believe they would also have decided who was going to be leading the negotiations, who was going to be doing the talking. Secondly, General Mladic was the senior of the Generals amongst his own Main Staff people, General Zivanovic and General Krstic; therefore, it's not surprising that he takes the leading role. Although I've not met General Mladic, by reputation and by what one's read and seen of him, he's that kind of large, dominant character that I would not expected to have sat quietly in a corner and allowed someone else to conduct the discussions. So it doesn't surprise me at all that he's taking the leading part in those discussions. I think that's a human aspect, and his large blustering, I call it, bullying character, I think, probably would mean that he was likely to be the main spokesman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another question. I don't know for the moment whether it is an order coming from the Main Staff to the Drina Corps and all the other brigades - you will remember there was something very urgent - or whether it was the Drina Corps repeating an order for the subordinate units. There is a point where it is noted "For Information," and then in brackets it says: [In English] "To be handed directly to the Commander or Chief of Staff." [Interpretation] This phrase in brackets, can that serve to confirm what you have told us, that in certain circumstances the Commander or his Assistant Commander or Chief of Staff were more or less the same thing?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: If your question is on that particular phrase, then I believe it does confirm exactly that; that there is this unique and special relationship between the Commander and the Chief of Staff. It doesn't take anything away from the Commander as the boss, as the number 1. But the Chief of Staff has a very special relationship to him, and people recognise that you can tell something to the Chief of Staff and you're effectively telling it to the Commander, so they are bracketed together in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another question. We have seen that for the purpose of communication and information, there were direct relations between the Assistants for Security in the Main Staff and in the Drina Corps. Have you come across documents containing orders; that is to say, is it necessary to make a distinction between information and orders?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, when you say have I come across documents, do you mean regulations or just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Orders. Have you seen any documents containing orders that were passed directly between two Assistants for Security?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe I have, sir, no. I'm just trying to think whether I have. I think I have seen, as I mentioned before, communications between the two facilitating a passage of information. I don't think I can recall seeing an order. If I could just remind you, Your Honour, of one comment I made about the Jankovic piece of paper - I'm afraid I can't remember the exhibit number - but there was a postscript, and I think I said yesterday, "You should take it as an order." Therefore, what that is saying to me is that it's not an order but take it as an order, recognising that there's no legitimate means for one Security Branch to order another but that you should take it as an order, meaning it's not an order but I think you should do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, just to summarise and maybe to finish off this question, there's another point. Seeing communications between the Assistant for Security from the Main Staff and the Assistant for Security in the Drina Corps, one can agree that information is circulating; that is to say, is it necessary to make a distinction between orders which may or may not be passed on directly, or information which can always be passed on from one to the other?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS RICHARD DANNATT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, the point that I want to make and I want to stay with is that it's perfectly legitimate, and I have seen several examples of information being passed from the Security Staff at one level to the Security Staff at another. I have seen no orders being passed from one level to another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
